USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the existing Section 301 structure ($50B at 25% plus List 3 at 10%) and use the already-scheduled January 1, 2019 step-up to 25% as bargaining leverage at the Trump–Xi G20 meeting. Do not announce a new $257B consumer-goods tranche before Buenos Aires, and do not roll back tariffs or commit to purchases until Beijing tables enforceable IP/tech-transfer remedies. Explore a pause or delay of the January hike only in exchange for a time-bound, verifiable work program — not atmospherics from a phone call.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is a modest US opportunity, not an existential hit. Combined 301 coverage is already ~$250B (timeline 2018-09-24) while China has only been able to match with ~$60B at 5–10% plus the earlier $50B pairing; that asymmetry, plus a still-solid US real economy (industrial production 104.07, Michigan sentiment 97.5, CPI only +0.6% over the window), is the core of the leverage. China is showing more strain: CNY has weakened ~9% to 6.92, reserves are down ~1.6%, and industrial production growth has slipped to 5.4% y/y. That is opportunity terrain (closer to the -0.5 leverage anchor than to +0.5 GDP-drag), but it is not a clear-opportunity -0.5 because US goods exports to China have already fallen ~20% (EXPCH 10.86B → 8.65B), soybean/farm retaliation forced a $12B USDA aid package with $3.6B earmarked for soy, and a 9% yuan move is blunting some tariff bite. Action should stay at negotiate (0.0), not escalate: a G20 meeting is already scheduled after the Nov 1 Trump–Xi call, Kudlow has said the US is “not on the cusp of a deal,” and the January 25% hike plus the threatened remaining ~$257B already constitute unused leverage. Further escalation now would land on consumer goods, risk another October-style VIX spike (VIX hit 25.23 on Oct 24), and give Beijing an easy walk-away at Buenos Aires. Midterms (Democrats take the House) do not constrain a China-hawk posture — bipartisan support for tougher IP enforcement remains — so there is no political need to concede, and no need to fire the next salvo before testing whether Xi will put a real offer on the table.
key_factors: Asymmetric tariff coverage: ~$250B US 301 vs ~$60B Chinese List-3 retaliation
G20 Trump-Xi meeting already scheduled after Nov 1 call; Jan 1 List-3 hike to 25% is unused leverage
US real economy still firm (IP, sentiment) while EXPCH is down ~20% and soy/farm aid is live
CNY -9% and slipping Chinese reserves/IP growth show Beijing is absorbing more pain
Kudlow: not on the cusp of a deal; mixed White House signals argue against premature rollback or a new $257B tranche
Post-midterm House flip does not weaken bipartisan China-hawk consensus

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory.
US goods exports to mainland China fell from $10.86B (Jun) to $8.65B (Nov), about -20% over the window.
CNY weakened from 6.34 to 6.92 per USD (~+9.2%), offsetting part of the tariff wedge.
Michigan consumer sentiment still high at 97.5 (Nov), only a modest dip from 98.2.
US industrial production 104.07 in Nov, up ~0.8% over the window — no recession signal.
VIX spiked to 25.23 on 2018-10-24 then eased to 16.36 by Nov 7 — markets are sensitive to escalation risk.
China industrial production growth slowed from 6.0% y/y in June to 5.4% in November.
Trump is poised to increase tariffs on $200B of Chinese imports to 25% from 10% starting Jan 1, and has threatened tariffs on all remaining Chinese imports.
Kudlow: 'We are not on the cusp of a deal'; officials said they are not yet at a place to start formally drafting a trade deal.
USDA to pay $4.7B from a $12B aid package; more than $3.6B to soybean farmers after China, which bought nearly a third of US soy in 2017, retaliated.
Democrats take the House but both parties support a tougher stance on Chinese trade/IP; Oval Office retains unilateral tariff authority.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the scheduled Trump–Xi G20 meeting to reopen talks aimed at freezing the January 1, 2019 jump of List 3 from 10% to 25% and blocking a further tranche on remaining Chinese exports. Do not add new tariffs or non-tariff measures before Buenos Aires, and do not pre-commit to large purchase packages or structural IP/tech reforms until the US matches with a concrete tariff pause. Keep existing retaliation in place as bargaining stock; fight and talk at the same time.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. Combined US Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B after List 3 took effect at 10% on 24 Sep 2018, with the rate scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 Jan 2019 and Trump threatening tariffs on the remaining ~$257B if G20 talks fail. That hits major export sectors just as official manufacturing PMI slipped to 50.2 in October, new export orders contracted for a fifth month (46.9), and Q3 GDP slowed to 6.5% — the weakest since 2009. The yuan has depreciated ~9% since mid-May (DEXCHUS 6.336 to 6.917), reserves have slipped ~1.6% to $3.08T, and industrial production growth has eased from 6.0% to 5.4% YoY. Firm-level tech pressure is real (ZTE denial order in April; NDAA ban on Huawei/ZTE for US government use) even if Huawei is not yet on the entity list. This is the CHN +0.5 band (export hit, FX pressure, firm targeting) tempered because reserves remain large, IP is still expanding, List 3 is only 10% today, and a G20 channel reopened on 1 Nov. Action should not escalate: China has already matched with duties on ~$110B of US goods (including soybeans) and has little remaining US import base to tax, while a new Chinese move would give Washington a pretext to cover the rest of Chinese exports. Nor should Beijing replay May 19, when a purchase-increase joint statement was followed ten days later by collapse of the truce and the $50B/$200B cascade. Negotiate without new commitments is the stance that uses the G20 window against the January cliff without paying upfront.
key_factors: US Section 301 now covers ~$250B; List 3 at 10% scheduled to 25% on 1 Jan 2019
Trump threat of remaining ~$257B if G20 talks fail
Trump-Xi 1 Nov call scheduled a G20 Argentina meeting — first live off-ramp since May truce collapse
China already retaliated on ~$110B (soy, autos, aircraft, then 5–10% on ~$60B); little unused US import ammunition
Yuan ~9% weaker since May; reserves down ~1.6% to $3.08T; Oct PMI 50.2 and export orders 46.9
Q3 GDP 6.5% (slowest since 2009); IP growth eased to 5.4% YoY — stressed, not collapsing
ZTE denial order and NDAA/Huawei-ZTE government ban show tech containment beyond tariffs
May 19 purchase-only truce was pocketed then reversed on 29 May — do not pre-concede purchases

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
CNY/USD from 6.336 (2018-05-14) to 6.9174 (2018-11-07); +9.18% yuan depreciation over the window.
China reserves ex-gold $3.081T on 2018-11-01, down ~$50.5B (-1.61%) over the window.
China industrial production index 105.4 in Nov 2018 vs 106.0 in June — YoY growth easing, still positive.
US goods exports to mainland China fell from $10.86B (June) to $8.65B (Nov), -20.3% — Chinese retaliation is biting US exporters.

The meeting in Buenos Aires could be a crucial turning point. Trump is poised to increase tariffs on $200B of Chinese imports to 25% from 10% starting Jan. 1. He has also threatened tariffs on all remaining imports from China.

Official manufacturing PMI fell to 50.2 in October (lowest in more than two years); new export orders contracted a fifth month to 46.9. Analysts warn front-loading now and a sharper export/employment hit after the January 25% hike.
China grew 6.5% in Q3 2018, weakest quarterly growth since early 2009, under pressure from debt-control and US tariffs on more than $250B of exports.

Trump said trade discussions were "moving along nicely" and planned to meet Xi at the G20; also warned he had billions of dollars of new tariffs ready if a deal did not materialize. China has retaliatory duties on $110B of US goods.
